citation: Hanley, J. A. and McNeil, B. J. (1982), The Meaning and Use of the Area under a Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) Curve, Radiology 143(1), 29-36, DOI 10.1148/radiology.143.1.7063747. The area is Table II, p. 31, whose bottom line reads `W = theta-hat = total (5) / (n_N * n_A) = 2,642/(58 x 51) = 0.893 = 89.3%`. The two counts are the row totals of Table I, p. 30: 58 truly normal images and 51 truly abnormal ones.
notes:
THE PUBLISHED AREA IS A RATIO OF TWO PUBLISHED INTEGERS, WHICH IS WHY THIS CASE CAN CLAIM MORE THAN THREE DECIMALS. Table II prints `0.893`, and a comparison against three printed decimals would sit outside every class in _policy.json -- the body returns 0.8931710615280595, which is 1.9156e-04 relative from 0.893, nearly twice the `estimate-1e-4` band. But the same line prints the WHOLE calculation: the Mann-Whitney total is 2,642 and the denominator is 58 x 51, so the page publishes the area as the exact rational 2642/2958. MEASURED in this worktree's environment: 2642.0/2958.0 evaluates to 0.8931710615280595 and `sklearn.metrics.roc_auc_score` returns the same double, so the disagreement is 0.0 exactly. Summing the tie-aware kernel of the paper's section IV over the 51 x 58 pairs also returns 2642.0, so the numerator is reproduced as well as the ratio.

WHY statistic-1e-6 AND NOT exact. The agreement measured today is bit-for-bit, and `exact` would be admissible at load time and would pass. It is refused because the library's route to this double and the page's are different arithmetic, and their landing on the same bit is a property of this build. MEASURED against scikit-learn 1.9.0: `roc_auc_score` calls `roc_curve` and then `auc`, a trapezoid over the curve's points, and on these 109 rows over five distinct ratings that curve has FIVE points -- so the area is a five-term trapezoid and not the 2958-term pairwise sum an earlier note here described. 2958 is the number of case-control PAIRS, which is what the paper's own kernel and this file's independent witness sum, and it is not what the library does. Pinning a bit across two such routes is a promise about a summation order that no source makes. `statistic-1e-6` is what the number actually is: a closed-form rank statistic whose only error is floating-point summation order, which is that class's own description. The class BITES on this payload -- MEASURED, ten times its tolerance moves 0.8931710615280595 to 0.8931799932386748, 51 to 51.000510000000006 and 58 to 58.00058000000001, and the comparison refuses all three -- so nothing here is admitted by a tolerance too loose to fail.

WHY THE TWO COUNTS ARE CLAIMED BESIDE IT. They are printed as the row totals of Table I and they are what makes the area's denominator checkable: 58 x 51 = 2958 is the number the published ratio divides by. They also make the case sensitive to the perturbation control in the way that matters -- see the paragraph below.

WHAT MOVES WHEN THE DATASET MOVES, because a green case proves nothing on its own. `hanley_mcneil_1982_ct_image_truth` is a column of 0 and 1, so the harness perturbs it by NEGATION: cases and controls swap, the area becomes 0.10682893847194047 and `n_cases` becomes 58. All three claimed fields therefore move, and the comparison refuses the moved payload. The rating column is perturbed by adding one to each integer, which is a shift of an ordinal score and leaves every area unchanged. HAD THE RESPONSE BEEN TRANSCRIBED AS THE WORDS THE TABLE PRINTS, THIS CASE WOULD NOT EXIST RATHER THAN SIT HERE PASSING: `move_leaf` appends `~` to a string, which leaves `abnormal` and `normal` in the same sort order, so -- MEASURED -- the area and both counts are identical before and after, only `controls_level` and `cases_level` move, and both of those are in `unchecked_keys` above. The control asserts that the moved payload must DISAGREE, so it would fail with an AssertionError. An earlier note here said the control would have examined nothing; the mechanism was right and the consequence was not. That is recorded in the truth dataset's own notes.

auc_ci IS UNCHECKED AND THE REASON IS NOT PRECISION. The paper prints a standard error of 0.032 for these data, and it is NOT DeLong's. It is Hanley and McNeil's own moment estimator, their Formula (1) on p. 32, evaluated at the Q1 = 0.8182 and Q2 = 0.8313 of Table II. MEASURED on the committed fixtures: that formula with the paper's own Q1 and Q2 returns 0.03200416314832256, reproducing the printed 3.2%, while the DeLong variance this body reports returns a standard error of 0.030724408379381122 -- a disagreement of 4.0 % relative, 400 times outside `estimate-1e-4`. The two estimators also disagree about their own ingredients: computed from the placement values, Q1 is 0.8288830990184423 and Q2 is 0.81607538214745 against the page's 0.8182 and 0.8313, because Table II's counting scheme handles the ties in this five-point scale differently from the placement-value moments. Quoting 0.032 as the DeLong standard error would be a false claim about which estimator produced it, and DeLong, DeLong and Clarke-Pearson (1988) publish no interval for this dataset. So the interval is reported and is not claimed here; the body's arithmetic for it is checked instead against the direct Mann-Whitney kernel, in tests/wrappers/c16_limited_dependent/test_roc_auc_binary.py.

WHAT ELSE THIS CASE DOES NOT CLAIM. `roc_curve` and `best_threshold` are derivable from Table I but are not printed in it, so they are exercised by the module's own tests rather than asserted against a page. `controls_level`, `cases_level`, `direction` and `percent` carry no number at all: they record which label this node treated as the case and which orientation it used, which is this engine's reporting decision and not the paper's.
